updates.summary: Germany's law implementing the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). It makes the Bundesnetzagentur the main market surveillance authority, single point of contact and central complaints office; BaFin supervises AI systems linked to regulated financial activities, and existing product regulators cover AI in products under Annex I. An independent AI market surveillance chamber oversees certain high-risk systems, including biometric systems used for law enforcement, border management, justice and democracy. The law also sets up a coordination and competence centre, AI regulatory sandboxes, approval of real-world tests of high-risk systems, fines and a register of certain high-risk systems.
updates.notes: The Federal Government sent its bill to the Bundesrat on 13 February 2026 as particularly urgent, noting that Germany had to implement the AI Act by 2 August 2025 (Bundesrat printed paper 97/26). The Bundestag passed the act on 11 June 2026, and on 10 July 2026 the Bundesrat decided not to call the mediation committee. The act was signed on 22 July 2026 and published in Bundesgesetzblatt 2026 I No. 223 on 28 July 2026; under its Article 5 it entered into force the day after promulgation, 29 July 2026. The KI-MIG is Article 1 of that act (Gesetz zur Durchführung der Verordnung über künstliche Intelligenz); Articles 2 to 4 amend the Whistleblower Protection Act to cover breaches of the AI Act, the First Book of the Social Code and the Financial Services Supervision Act. Structure of the KI-MIG: Part 1 scope; Part 2 competent authorities and cooperation (sections 2-10); Part 3 powers (section 11); Part 4 innovation support (sections 12-14, AI regulatory sandboxes and real-world testing of high-risk systems); Part 5 fines (sections 15-17); Part 6 retention duties; Part 7 evaluation; Part 8 register of certain high-risk AI systems (section 20). Breaches listed in section 15 carry fines of up to EUR 50,000, and no fines are imposed on public authorities and other public bodies (section 17(2)). A real-world test plan counts as approved if the provider receives no answer within 30 days. The AI market surveillance chamber reports to the Bundestag every year, first for 2026; the government evaluates the supervisory structure within 18 months and again within three years of entry into force.

updates.summary: Dutch government-wide vision on generative AI, sent to the House of Representatives in January 2024. It maps opportunities and risks, including mis- and disinformation and deepfakes, bias and discrimination, dependence on a few US technology companies, misuse and systemic security risks, and reviews the law, notably the EU AI Act. Four principles: generative AI is developed and applied safely and equitably, serves human welfare and safeguards autonomy, and contributes to sustainability and prosperity. Six action lines: collaborate, monitor developments, shape and apply laws and regulations, increase knowledge and skills, innovate, and strong and clear supervision and enforcement.

Other annexes to that letter are an overview of related motions and commitments and a request for advice to the Social and Economic Council (SER) on AI, the future of work and its socio-economic implications. The vision responds to a motion adopted by the House in April 2023. On 22 April 2025 State Secretary Szabó presented to the House a government-wide position on the use of generative AI in government, with a government-wide guide on its responsible use.

updates.summary: First decree under Article 24 of Law 132/2025 adapting Italian law to the AI Act. Title I governs police AI use under the principles of proportionality, non-discrimination, human oversight and transparency, including real-time remote biometric identification and retrospective facial recognition with judicial authorisation. Article 12 adds Article 437-bis to the Criminal Code; failing to adopt required safety or human-oversight measures for high-risk AI systems carries one to five years in prison if it endangers life or safety. Articles 16-20 let courts order disclosure of evidence on an AI system, presume causation on breach of an AI Act obligation and allow direct action against insurers.
updates.notes: Approved in preliminary form by the Council of Ministers on 10 June 2026 and finally on 4 August 2026, after opinions of the data protection authority (Garante), the Unified Conference (20 July 2026) and the competent parliamentary committees; issued on 9 September 2026, published in GU n. 214 of 15 September 2026 and in force from 30 September 2026. 22 articles in three titles. Where the danger is to the security of the State, the new offence carries two to eight years; altering a high-risk AI system is a separate offence. Article 15 makes companies liable under Legislative Decree 231/2001 for the new offence. Compliance with the AI Act, even if certified, does not by itself exclude liability (Article 19). Police AI systems already contracted, under development or testing, or in use must be brought into line with Chapter II of Title I within one year of entry into force.

updates.summary: Italy's second legislative decree implementing the EU AI Act under Law 132/2025. AgID is the notifying authority; ACN is the market surveillance authority and single point of contact, with the Bank of Italy, CONSOB and IVASS for high-risk AI used in financial services and the data protection authority within Article 74(8) of the AI Act. ACN has inspection powers, including unannounced checks on real-world testing. Fines follow the AI Act ceilings and add up to EUR 1 million or 0.5% of turnover for breaches of Articles 27 and 86. AgID and ACN run a national AI sandbox. Employers must leave final employment decisions to a person, and workplace AI enters the occupational risk assessment.
updates.notes: Adopted under Article 24 of Law 132/2025 after a preliminary deliberation of the Council of Ministers on 10 June 2026, the opinions of AgID, ACN, the data protection authority, the Unified Conference and the parliamentary committees, and a final deliberation on 4 August 2026; issued on 7 October 2026, published in Gazzetta Ufficiale, Serie Generale n. 234, of 8 October 2026, and in force from 23 October 2026. It has 54 articles in five chapters. ACN registers the Annex III point 2 high-risk systems nationally; a coordinating committee at the Prime Minister's Office sets the sandbox's priorities, and sandboxes for dual-use and judicial AI are to follow by regulation. Follow-up acts are due within 90 days (teacher training, costs of market surveillance), six months (AI training in the professions and in continuing medical education) and twelve months (parameters adjusting professionals' fair compensation to the risk class of the AI they use). Article 52 makes data, algorithms and mathematical methods for training AI systems protectable as trade secrets under the industrial property code.
